reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: FKRP mutations cause a broad phenotypic spectrum, from a milder limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (formerly LGMD2I, now LGMDR9) to a severe congenital muscular dystrophy (MDC1C) with brain and eye involvement
The limb-girdle form typically presents with proximal lower-limb and pelvic-girdle weakness, sometimes with calf hypertrophy resembling a dystrophinopathy
Serum creatine kinase is usually substantially elevated across the spectrum
Inherited in an autosomal recessive manner as one of the alpha-dystroglycanopathies caused by defective glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan
Cardiomyopathy and respiratory muscle weakness are important complications even in ambulant patients with the milder phenotype
The severe congenital end may include structural brain malformation and eye abnormalities, overlapping with the Walker-Warburg and muscle-eye-brain phenotypes
Because cardiac and respiratory involvement can be disproportionate to limb weakness, structured surveillance of the heart and respiratory function is essential
reference.pathophysiology: FKRP-related dystroglycanopathy is caused by biallelic mutations in FKRP, encoding fukutin-related protein, an enzyme involved in the glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan. Alpha-dystroglycan is a central component of the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex, and its sugar chains bind extracellular-matrix ligands such as laminin to link the muscle-fibre cytoskeleton to the basement membrane. Defective glycosylation weakens this linkage, so the sarcolemma is mechanically vulnerable and undergoes repeated injury and degeneration, producing a dystrophic phenotype. The severity depends on how profoundly glycosylation is impaired, ranging from a relatively mild limb-girdle dystrophy to a severe congenital form in which deficient dystroglycan function also disrupts neuronal migration and eye development.
additionalDifferentials: Other dystroglycanopathies (e.g. fukutin, POMT1/2, POMGNT1 related)
Other congenital muscular dystrophies including merosin-deficient forms
Metabolic myopathies with high creatine kinase
additionalInvestigations: Serum creatine kinase, typically markedly elevated
Muscle biopsy with immunohistochemistry showing reduced glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan
Targeted FKRP genetic testing, or a dystroglycanopathy or limb-girdle gene panel
Cardiac assessment with electrocardiogram and echocardiography
Respiratory function testing including overnight monitoring
Brain and orbital imaging in the congenital/severe phenotype
redFlags: Cardiomyopathy or heart failure, which may be out of proportion to limb weakness
Respiratory muscle weakness with nocturnal hypoventilation
In infants, structural brain malformation, seizures or visual impairment indicating the severe phenotype
Loss of ambulation requiring orthopaedic and rehabilitation planning
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on where on the spectrum a patient sits, from a relatively slowly progressive limb-girdle dystrophy compatible with prolonged ambulation and near-normal lifespan to a severe congenital form with early respiratory and neurological compromise; cardiac and respiratory surveillance materially improves outcomes across the range.
pitfalls: Neglecting cardiac and respiratory monitoring in an ambulant patient with the milder phenotype
Mistaking calf hypertrophy and high creatine kinase for a dystrophinopathy without genetic confirmation
Assuming normal cognition and vision exclude the diagnosis, since these are only affected at the severe end
Not recognising the wide phenotypic range attributable to the same gene
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Physiotherapy, orthoses and mobility aids to preserve ambulation and manage proximal and pelvic-girdle weakness
Cardiac surveillance with ECG and echocardiography, with heart-failure therapy for cardiomyopathy even in ambulant patients
Respiratory monitoring including overnight oximetry, with non-invasive ventilation for nocturnal hypoventilation and respiratory muscle weakness
Management of the severe congenital phenotype with developmental support and ophthalmological and neurological care for associated brain malformation and eye abnormalities
Genetic counselling and FKRP testing given autosomal recessive inheritance, with carrier testing of relatives and reproductive counselling
Multidisciplinary neuromuscular, cardiology and respiratory care with regular review
Escalation for cardiac decompensation or respiratory failure
